name: Chapter 2: Electrochemistry
description: Galvanic cells, electrode potentials, Nernst equation, Gibbs energy, conductivity, Kohlrausch law, electrolysis, batteries, fuel cells, corrosion

cards.term: What is electrochemistry?
cards.definition: Study of producing electricity from spontaneous reactions and using electricity to drive non-spontaneous ones

cards.term: Galvanic cell vs electrolytic cell: energy conversion?
cards.definition: Galvanic: chemical → electrical (spontaneous, ΔG < 0). Electrolytic: electrical → chemical (non-spontaneous).

cards.term: Cell reaction and emf of the Daniell cell?
cards.definition: \[Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu\]1.1 V at unit concentrations

cards.term: Figure 2.1 · Daniell cell
External voltage opposing a Daniell cell: E<sub>ext</sub> < 1.1 V, = 1.1 V, > 1.1 V?
cards.definition:
< 1.1 V: works as a galvanic cell
= 1.1 V: no current, no reaction
> 1.1 V: reaction reverses (Zn deposits, Cu dissolves): electrolytic cell

cards.term: Intuition: what does E<sub>ext</sub> = 1.1 V tell you about the cell?
cards.definition: The opposing push exactly balances the reaction’s own "push"; so emf is the maximum voltage the reaction can supply

cards.term: Correction/footnote: concentration or activity in the Nernst equation?
cards.definition: Strictly activity; it equals concentration only in dilute solutions

cards.term: Half-reactions in the Daniell cell and where they occur?
cards.definition: Reduction \( Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu \) at copper; oxidation \( Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^- \) at zinc

cards.term: What is a half-cell (redox couple)?
cards.definition: A metal electrode dipped in its electrolyte; the reduction half-cell and the oxidation half-cell

cards.term: When is a salt bridge not needed?
cards.definition: When both electrodes dip in the same electrolyte

cards.term: Why is a salt bridge needed? (teacher addition)
cards.definition:
It completes the circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral.
Without it, charge builds up and current stops at once

cards.term: What is electrode potential?
cards.definition: The potential difference between an electrode and its electrolyte, from the balance of metal → ion and ion → metal tendencies

cards.term: What is standard electrode potential?
cards.definition:
Electrode potential when all species are at unit concentration (gases 1 bar), usually 298 K.
IUPAC: standard reduction potential

cards.text: In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the {{c1::anode}}, which is {{c2::negative}}; reduction occurs at the {{c3::cathode}}, which is {{c4::positive}}.

cards.term: Direction of electron flow and current in the external circuit?
cards.definition: Electrons: anode → cathode (− to +). Current: the opposite direction.

cards.term: Mnemonic for anode and cathode?
cards.definition: An Ox, Red Cat: ANode = OXidation, REDuction = CAThode. True in every cell.

cards.term: Anode and cathode signs in the two cell types
cards.definition: Galvanic cell: anode: − (negative); Galvanic cell: cathode: + (positive); Electrolytic cell: anode: + (connected to battery +); Electrolytic cell: cathode: − (connected to battery −)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Sign trap

Sign of the electrode?

Galvanic cell: anode?
Galvanic cell: cathode?
Electrolytic cell: anode?
Electrolytic cell: cathode?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Sign trap

Sign of the electrode?

Galvanic cell: anode− (negative)
Galvanic cell: cathode+ (positive)
Electrolytic cell: anode+ (connected to battery +)
Electrolytic cell: cathode− (connected to battery −)

Oxidation is always at the anode; only the sign flips, because in electrolysis the battery forces electrons in.

cards.term: Intuition: why is the galvanic anode negative?
cards.definition: Oxidation there releases electrons into the metal, so electrons pile up: it is the electron source (−)

cards.term: Cell potential vs emf?
cards.definition: Both = E(cathode) − E(anode); called emf when no current is drawn

cards.term: Cell notation convention?
cards.definition: Anode on the left, cathode on the right | = phase boundary || = salt bridge e.g. Cu|Cu²⁺||Ag⁺|Ag

cards.term: Formula for E<sub>cell</sub> from electrode potentials?
cards.definition: \[E_{cell} = E_{right} - E_{left} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode}\](both as reduction potentials)

cards.term: Trap: in Ecell = Ecathode − Eanode, do you reverse the anode’s sign as well?
cards.definition: No: use both reduction potentials as listed; the minus sign already accounts for the anode being an oxidation

cards.term: Why can’t a single electrode potential be measured?
cards.definition: A voltmeter needs two electrodes; only differences can be measured, so a reference is chosen

cards.term: Standard hydrogen electrode (SHE): notation and potential?
cards.definition: Pt(s)|H₂(g, 1 bar)|H⁺(aq, 1 M); assigned 0 V at all temperatures

cards.term: Figure 2.3 · Standard hydrogen electrode

masks.answer: Finely divided platinum coated on platinum foil

cards.term: Construction of SHE?
cards.definition: Pt electrode coated with platinum black, dipped in 1 M acid, pure H₂ bubbled at 1 bar

cards.term: How is E° of Cu²⁺/Cu measured?
cards.definition: SHE as anode (left), Cu half-cell as cathode: measured emf 0.34 V = E°

cards.term: E° of Zn²⁺/Zn and its meaning?
cards.definition: −0.76 V: H⁺ can oxidise Zn (Zn dissolves in acids)

cards.term: Why doesn’t Cu dissolve in HCl, but does in HNO₃?
cards.definition: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) > 0, so H⁺ cannot oxidise Cu; in HNO₃ the nitrate ion is the oxidant

cards.term: E° of Daniell cell from E° values?
cards.definition: 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V

cards.term: Role of Pt or Au as inert electrodes?
cards.definition: Provide a surface for the redox reaction and conduct electrons, without reacting (H₂ electrode, Br₂ electrode)

cards.term: Positive E° means the reduced form is…?
cards.definition: More stable than H₂; the couple is a weaker reducing agent than H⁺/H₂

cards.term: Strongest oxidising agent and strongest reducing agent in Table 2.1?
cards.definition: F₂ (E° = +2.87 V); Li (E° = −3.05 V)

cards.term: Going down Table 2.1 (E° decreasing): trend?
cards.definition: Oxidising power of the left-side species falls; reducing power of the right-side species rises

cards.term: Intuition: how to read E° as a "tug of war" for electrons?
cards.definition: Higher E° = grabs electrons harder (gets reduced). In any pair, the higher-E° couple is reduced, the lower one is oxidised

cards.term: Can CuSO₄ be stored in a zinc pot? (Intext 2.2)
cards.definition: No: E°(Zn) < E°(Cu), so Zn reduces Cu²⁺ and the pot dissolves

cards.term: Three substances that can oxidise Fe²⁺? (Intext 2.3)
cards.definition: Any with E° > 0.77 V: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, MnO₄⁻/H⁺, Cr₂O₇²⁻/H⁺, H₂O₂

cards.term: Uses of electrochemical cells (NCERT list)?
cards.definition: Finding pH, solubility product, equilibrium constants, thermodynamic data; potentiometric titrations

cards.term: Nernst equation for Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ → M?
cards.definition: \[E = E^{\circ} - \frac{RT}{nF} \ln \frac{1}{[M^{n+}]}\]

cards.term: Nernst equation for a cell at 298 K?
cards.definition: \[E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \frac{0.059}{n} \log Q\]

cards.term: Where does 0.059 V come from?
Nernst equation for the Daniell cell?
How does E<sub>cell</sub> of Daniell cell change with [Cu²⁺] and [Zn²⁺]?
cards.definition: Rises with more Cu²⁺ (reactant), falls with more Zn²⁺ (product)

cards.term: Intuition: Nernst equation = Le Chatelier?
cards.definition:
More reactant pushes the reaction forward, so the cell "pushes" electrons harder (higher E).
More product pushes back

cards.term: What goes into Q in the Nernst equation?
cards.definition: Products over reactants with powers solids and pure liquids = 1 gases as partial pressures

cards.term: Trap: n for Ni + 2Ag⁺ → Ni²⁺ + 2Ag?
cards.definition: n = 2 (electrons transferred), and Q = [Ni²⁺]/[Ag⁺]²

cards.term: Potential of hydrogen electrode at pH 10? (Intext 2.4)
cards.definition: E = −0.059 × pH = −0.59 V

cards.term: Nernst: Mg–Ag cell

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.1

Mg + 2Ag⁺(0.0001 M) → Mg²⁺(0.130 M) + 2Ag; E° = 3.17 V. E_cell?

Cell: Mg|Mg²⁺(0.130 M)||Ag⁺(0.0001 M)|Ag; n = 2.
  1. Q = 0.130 / (0.0001)² = 1.3 × 10⁷
  2. log Q = 7.11
  3. ?
  4. = 2.96 V

cards.term: emf of Ni|Ni²⁺(0.160 M)||Ag⁺(0.002 M)|Ag, E° = 1.05 V? (Intext 2.5)
What happens to a Daniell cell’s voltage as it runs?
cards.definition: [Zn²⁺] rises, [Cu²⁺] falls, so E drops until E = 0 at equilibrium

cards.term: Relation between E°_cell and K?
cards.definition: \[E^{\circ}_{cell} = \frac{2.303 \, RT}{nF} \log K_C = \frac{0.059}{n} \log K_C\](298 K)

cards.term: K<sub>C</sub> for the Daniell cell reaction?
cards.definition: log K = 2 × 1.1/0.059 = 37.3, so KC ≈ 2 × 10³⁷: goes to completion

cards.term: K for Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag, E° = 0.46 V? (Example 2.2)
Intuition: why do small E° values give enormous K?
cards.definition: K depends on E° exponentially: every 0.059/n V multiplies K by 10

cards.term: Relation between ΔrG and E<sub>cell</sub>?
cards.definition: \( \Delta_r G = -nFE_{cell} \); standard: \( \Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell} \)

cards.term: Why is ΔrG = −nFE the maximum useful work?
cards.definition: Reversible work (charge nF moved through potential E) equals the decrease in Gibbs energy

cards.term: Spontaneous cell: signs of E and ΔG?
cards.definition: E > 0, ΔG < 0 (and K > 1)

cards.term: E<sub>cell</sub> is intensive; ΔrG is extensive. Consequence?
cards.definition: Doubling the equation doubles ΔG (n doubles) but E stays the same

cards.term: Trap: to balance 2Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Ag, do you double E°(Ag⁺/Ag)?
cards.definition: Never: E° is intensive (volts = energy per charge). Keep 0.80 V.

cards.term: Combining electrode potentials via ΔG

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Combining half-cells

E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = 0.77 V, E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V. E°(Fe³⁺/Fe)?

Potentials don’t add for a half-cell; ΔG does.
  1. ΔG₁ = −1·F·0.77 = −0.77F
  2. ΔG₂ = −2·F·(−0.44) = +0.88F
  3. ΔG₃ = ΔG₁ + ΔG₂ = +0.11F = −3F·E°
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Combining half-cells

E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = 0.77 V, E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V. E°(Fe³⁺/Fe)?

Potentials don’t add for a half-cell; ΔG does.
  1. ΔG₁ = −1·F·0.77 = −0.77F
  2. ΔG₂ = −2·F·(−0.44) = +0.88F
  3. ΔG₃ = ΔG₁ + ΔG₂ = +0.11F = −3F·E°
  4. E°(Fe³⁺/Fe) = −0.037 V

cards.term: ΔG° of the Daniell cell

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.3

Daniell cell, E° = 1.1 V. ΔrG°?

n = 2, F = 96487 C mol⁻¹.
  1. ΔrG° = −nFE°
  2. = −2 × 96487 × 1.1
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 2.3

Daniell cell, E° = 1.1 V. ΔrG°?

n = 2, F = 96487 C mol⁻¹.
  1. ΔrG° = −nFE°
  2. = −2 × 96487 × 1.1
  3. = −212,271 J mol⁻¹ = −212.27 kJ mol⁻¹

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Example 2.3 prints ΔrG° = −21227 J mol⁻¹. Right value?
cards.definition: −212,271 J mol⁻¹ (a digit is missing); the kJ value, −212.27, is correct

cards.term: ΔG° and K for 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, E° = 0.236 V? (Intext 2.6)
cards.definition: ΔG° = −2 × 96487 × 0.236 = −45.5 kJ/mol; log K = 8.0 → K ≈ 1 × 10⁸

cards.term: E°, ΔG° and K
cards.definition: E°cell > 0: ΔG°  1: forward favoured; E°cell = 0: ΔG° = 0, K = 1; E°cell < 0: ΔG° > 0, K < 1: reverse favoured

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Link

Spontaneity from each?

E°cell > 0?
E°cell = 0?
E°cell < 0?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Link

Spontaneity from each?

E°cell > 0ΔG° < 0, K > 1: forward favoured
E°cell = 0ΔG° = 0, K = 1
E°cell < 0ΔG° > 0, K < 1: reverse favoured

ΔG° = −nFE° = −RT ln K ties all three together.

cards.term: Resistance in terms of resistivity?
cards.definition: \[R = \rho \frac{l}{A}\]ρ in Ω m (1 Ω m = 100 Ω cm)

cards.term: Conductance G and conductivity κ?
cards.definition: \[G = \frac{1}{R} = \kappa \frac{A}{l}\]G in siemens (S = Ω⁻¹ = mho); κ = 1/ρ in S m⁻¹

cards.term: Unit conversion: 1 S cm⁻¹ = ? S m⁻¹
cards.definition: 100 S m⁻¹

cards.term: Metallic (electronic) conductance depends on?
cards.definition: Nature and structure of metal, number of valence electrons, temperature (decreases as T rises)

cards.term: Conductivity of pure water and why?
cards.definition: 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ S m⁻¹: only ~10⁻⁷ M H⁺ and OH⁻ from self-ionisation

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Table 2.2 lists metals at ~10³ S m⁻¹ (Cu 5.9 × 10³). Real values?
cards.definition: About 10⁷ S m⁻¹ (Cu ≈ 5.9 × 10⁷, Ag ≈ 6.2 × 10⁷); the table’s exponents are off by 10⁴

cards.text: Classes by conductivity: {{c1::conductors}} (metals, graphite), {{c2::insulators}} (glass, Teflon), {{c3::semiconductors}} (Si, doped Si, GaAs), {{c4::superconductors}} (zero resistivity).

cards.term: Superconductors: temperature range?
cards.definition: Metals/alloys at 0–15 K; some ceramics and mixed oxides up to ~150 K

cards.term: Conducting polymers: discovery and examples (box)?
cards.definition:
Polyacetylene doped with I₂ (MacDiarmid, Heeger, Shirakawa, Nobel 2000)
Also polyaniline, polypyrrole, polythiophene

cards.term: Ionic (electrolytic) conductivity depends on?
cards.definition:
Nature of electrolyte
Ion size and solvation
Solvent and its viscosity
Concentration
Temperature (increases with T)

cards.term: Intuition: why does heating raise ionic but lower metallic conductivity?
cards.definition: Hot solvent is less viscous, so ions move faster; in metals, hotter vibrating atoms scatter electrons more

cards.term: Metallic vs electrolytic conduction: effect on the conductor?
cards.definition: Metal: composition unchanged. Electrolyte: prolonged DC changes composition (electrolysis)

cards.term: Two problems in measuring resistance of a solution, and the fixes?
cards.definition: DC changes the solution → use AC. Solution can’t be clamped like a wire → use a conductivity cell.

cards.term: Why are the electrodes platinised (Pt black)?
cards.definition: Finely divided Pt gives a large surface; reduces polarisation errors (teacher note)

cards.term: What is the cell constant G*?
cards.definition: \[G^* = \frac{l}{A} = R \kappa\]unit length⁻¹; found using KCl solutions of known κ

cards.term: Wheatstone bridge for solutions: source and detector?
cards.definition: Oscillator O: AC at 550–5000 Hz detector P: headphone at balance\[R_2 = \frac{R_1 R_4}{R_3}\]

cards.term: Conductivity from cell constant?
cards.definition: \[\kappa = \frac{G^*}{R}\]

cards.term: Define molar conductivity.
cards.definition: \[\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa}{c}\]conductivity per unit molar concentration

cards.term: Λm in S cm² mol⁻¹ from κ in S cm⁻¹ and molarity M?
cards.definition: \[\Lambda_m = \frac{1000 \, \kappa}{M}\]

cards.term: 1 S m² mol⁻¹ = ? S cm² mol⁻¹
cards.definition: 10⁴

cards.term: Conductivity from cell constant
cards.definition: κ 0.248 S/m; Λm 124 S cm²/mol

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.4

Cell: 100 Ω with 0.1 M KCl (κ 1.29 S/m); 520 Ω with 0.02 M KCl. κ and Λm of 0.02 M KCl?

Find G* first.
  1. G* = κR = 1.29 × 100 = 129 m⁻¹
  2. ?
  3. c = 0.02 M = 20 mol m⁻³
  4. Λm = 0.248/20 = 124 × 10⁻⁴ S m² mol⁻¹ (124 S cm² mol⁻¹)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 2.4

Cell: 100 Ω with 0.1 M KCl (κ 1.29 S/m); 520 Ω with 0.02 M KCl. κ and Λm of 0.02 M KCl?

Find G* first.
  1. G* = κR = 1.29 × 100 = 129 m⁻¹
  2. κ = G*/R = 129/520 = 0.248 S m⁻¹
  3. c = 0.02 M = 20 mol m⁻³
  4. Λm = 0.248/20 = 124 × 10⁻⁴ S m² mol⁻¹ (124 S cm² mol⁻¹)

cards.term: Resistivity, conductivity and Λm of NaOH

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.5

0.05 M NaOH column: d = 1 cm, l = 50 cm, R = 5.55 × 10³ Ω. ρ, κ, Λm?

A = πr² = 0.785 cm².
  1. ρ = RA/l = 5550 × 0.785/50 = 87.1 Ω cm
  2. κ = 1/ρ = 0.01148 S cm⁻¹
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 2.5

0.05 M NaOH column: d = 1 cm, l = 50 cm, R = 5.55 × 10³ Ω. ρ, κ, Λm?

A = πr² = 0.785 cm².
  1. ρ = RA/l = 5550 × 0.785/50 = 87.1 Ω cm
  2. κ = 1/ρ = 0.01148 S cm⁻¹
  3. Λm = 1000 × 0.01148/0.05 = 229.6 S cm² mol⁻¹

cards.term: Effect of dilution on κ, and why?
cards.definition: κ decreases (strong and weak): fewer ions per unit volume

cards.term: Effect of dilution on Λm, and why?
cards.definition: Λm increases: Λm = κV, and the rise in V (volume holding 1 mol) outweighs the fall in κ

cards.term: Intuition: κ vs Λm on dilution?
cards.definition:
κ = current carriers in a fixed 1 cm³ box (fewer as you dilute).
Λm = all ions from 1 mole, wherever they are.
They are never lost, and on dilution they move more freely (and weak ones ionise more)

cards.term: What is limiting molar conductivity Λ°m?
cards.definition: Λm as concentration → zero (infinite dilution)

cards.term: Debye–Hückel–Onsager form for strong electrolytes?
cards.definition: \[\Lambda_m = \Lambda^{\circ}_m - A\sqrt{c}\]Λm vs √c is a straight line, intercept Λ°m, slope −A

cards.term: A depends on?
cards.definition: Solvent, temperature and electrolyte type (1-1 NaCl, 2-1 CaCl₂, 2-2 MgSO₄); same for all of one type

cards.term: Strong vs weak electrolyte: shape of Λm vs √c?
cards.definition: Strong (KCl): gentle straight line. Weak (CH₃COOH): steep rise near zero concentration.

cards.term: Why does Λm of a weak electrolyte rise so steeply on dilution?
cards.definition: Degree of dissociation α increases, creating many more ions per mole

cards.term: Why can’t Λ°m of a weak electrolyte be found by extrapolation?
cards.definition: The curve is steep and non-linear near c = 0, and at such dilution κ is too small to measure accurately

cards.term: Λ°m and A for KCl from Example 2.6?
cards.definition: Λ°m = 150.0 S cm² mol⁻¹; A = 87.46 S cm² mol⁻¹ (mol/L)⁻¹ᐟ²

cards.term: Kohlrausch’s observation?
cards.definition: Λ°(KX) − Λ°(NaX) ≈ 23.4 for any X; Λ°(NaBr) − Λ°(NaCl) ≈ 1.8 S cm² mol⁻¹: each ion contributes a fixed amount

cards.term: Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions?
cards.definition: Λ°m of an electrolyte = sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion:\[\Lambda^{\circ}_m = \nu_+ \lambda^{\circ}_+ + \nu_- \lambda^{\circ}_-\]

cards.term: Why are λ° of H⁺ (349.6) and OH⁻ (199.1) so high?
cards.definition: They hop along H-bonded water chains (Grotthuss mechanism) instead of moving bodily (teacher addition)

cards.term: Λ°m of CaCl₂ and MgSO₄? (Example 2.7)
cards.definition: CaCl₂: 119.0 + 2(76.3) = 271.6; MgSO₄: 106.0 + 160.0 = 266 S cm² mol⁻¹

cards.term: Kohlrausch: Λ° of acetic acid
cards.definition: 390.5 S cm²/mol

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.8

Λ° of NaCl, HCl, NaAc = 126.4, 425.9, 91.0. Λ°(HAc)?

Add and subtract so only H⁺ and Ac⁻ remain.
  1. ?
  2. = 425.9 + 91.0 − 126.4
  3. = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 2.8

Λ° of NaCl, HCl, NaAc = 126.4, 425.9, 91.0. Λ°(HAc)?

Add and subtract so only H⁺ and Ac⁻ remain.
  1. Λ°(HAc) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(NaAc) − Λ°(NaCl)
  2. = 425.9 + 91.0 − 126.4
  3. = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹

cards.term: Degree of dissociation from conductivity?
cards.definition: \( \alpha = \frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^{\circ}_m} \) and \( K_a = \frac{c\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} \)

cards.term: Ka of acetic acid from conductivity

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.9

κ of 0.001028 M acetic acid = 4.95 × 10⁻⁵ S cm⁻¹; Λ° = 390.5. Ka?

Λm = 1000κ/c.
  1. Λm = 4.95 × 10⁻⁵ × 1000/0.001028 = 48.15 S cm² mol⁻¹
  2. ?
  3. Ka = cα²/(1 − α)
  4. = 1.78 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 2.9

κ of 0.001028 M acetic acid = 4.95 × 10⁻⁵ S cm⁻¹; Λ° = 390.5. Ka?

Λm = 1000κ/c.
  1. Λm = 4.95 × 10⁻⁵ × 1000/0.001028 = 48.15 S cm² mol⁻¹
  2. α = 48.15/390.5 = 0.1233
  3. Ka = cα²/(1 − α)
  4. = 1.78 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹

cards.term: α and Ka of 0.025 M HCOOH, Λm = 46.1 (λ° H⁺ 349.6, HCOO⁻ 54.6)? (Intext 2.9)
cards.definition: Λ° = 404.2 α = 0.114 Ka = 0.025 × 0.114²/0.886 ≈ 3.67 × 10⁻⁴

cards.term: How to get Λ°m of water? (Intext 2.8)
cards.definition: λ°(H⁺) + λ°(OH⁻) = 548.7 S cm² mol⁻¹ (or Λ°HCl + Λ°NaOH − Λ°NaCl)

cards.term: Electrolysis of CuSO₄ with copper electrodes?
cards.definition: Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (deposits). Anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (dissolves).

cards.term: Electrolytic refining of copper?
cards.definition: Impure Cu = anode (dissolves); pure Cu deposits on the cathode

cards.term: Why are Na, Mg, Al made electrolytically? How?
cards.definition: No suitable chemical reducing agent. Na, Mg: fused chlorides; Al: Al₂O₃ with cryolite

cards.term: Faraday’s first law?
cards.definition: Amount of reaction at an electrode ∝ quantity of electricity passed (w = ZQ)

cards.term: Faraday’s second law?
cards.definition: For the same charge, amounts liberated ∝ equivalent weights (atomic mass ÷ electrons needed)

cards.term: Charge passed by a current?
cards.definition: \( Q = I t \) (C = A × s)

cards.term: What is 1 Faraday?
cards.definition: Charge on 1 mol electrons = 96487 ≈ 96500 C mol⁻¹

cards.term: Faradays to deposit 1 mol Ag, Mg, Al?
cards.definition: 1F, 2F, 3F (electrons in the half-reaction)

cards.term: Faradays per second at 50,000 A?
cards.definition: ≈ 0.518 F s⁻¹

cards.term: Mass of Cu deposited

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.10

CuSO₄ electrolysed 10 min at 1.5 A. Mass of Cu?

Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (63 g needs 2F).
  1. Q = 1.5 × 600 = 900 C
  2. ?
  3. mol Cu = 0.00466
  4. mass = 0.00466 × 63 = 0.2938 g
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 2.10

CuSO₄ electrolysed 10 min at 1.5 A. Mass of Cu?

Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (63 g needs 2F).
  1. Q = 1.5 × 600 = 900 C
  2. mol e⁻ = 900/96487 = 0.00933
  3. mol Cu = 0.00466
  4. mass = 0.00466 × 63 = 0.2938 g

cards.term: Electrons through a wire at 0.5 A for 2 h? (Intext 2.10)
Charge to reduce 1 mol Cr₂O₇²⁻ to Cr³⁺? (Intext 2.12)
cards.definition: 6 mol e⁻ = 6F = 5.79 × 10⁵ C

cards.term: Trap: 1 mol electrons at the cathode deposits how many moles of H₂, Cu, Al?
cards.definition: ½, ½, ⅓ mol respectively

cards.term: Products of electrolysis depend on?
cards.definition: Material electrolysed, electrode type (inert vs reactive), competing E° values, and overpotential

cards.term: What is overpotential?
cards.definition: Extra voltage needed because some feasible electrode reactions are kinetically slow

cards.term: Products of electrolysis of molten NaCl?
cards.definition: Na at cathode, Cl₂ at anode

cards.term: Products of electrolysis of aqueous NaCl?
cards.definition: H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode, NaOH in solution

cards.term: Why H₂ and not Na at the cathode (aq NaCl)?
cards.definition: Higher E° is reduced first: H⁺/H₂ 0.00 V ≫ Na⁺/Na −2.71 V; net H₂O + e⁻ → ½H₂ + OH⁻

cards.term: Why Cl₂ and not O₂ at the anode (aq NaCl), though O₂ has lower E° (1.23 vs 1.36 V)?
cards.definition: Oxygen evolution has a high overpotential, so Cl⁻ is oxidised in practice

cards.term: Rule of thumb for electrolysis products (intuition)?
cards.definition: Cathode: the species easiest to reduce (highest E°). Anode: the species easiest to oxidise (lowest E°), unless overpotential interferes.

cards.term: Anode product for dilute vs concentrated H₂SO₄?
cards.definition: Dilute: O₂ (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, 1.23 V). Concentrated: S₂O₈²⁻ (peroxodisulphate, 1.96 V).

cards.term: Trap: aqueous CuSO₄ with inert Pt electrodes gives?
cards.definition: Cu at cathode, O₂ at anode (solution turns acidic); with Cu electrodes the anode dissolves instead

cards.term: What makes a battery practical?
cards.definition: Light, compact, and voltage steady during use

cards.term: Primary vs secondary battery?
cards.definition: Primary: reaction occurs once, not rechargeable (dry cell). Secondary: rechargeable (lead storage, Ni–Cd).

cards.term: Dry (Leclanché) cell: anode, cathode, electrolyte?
cards.definition: Anode: Zn container. Cathode: graphite rod in MnO₂ + carbon. Electrolyte: moist paste of NH₄Cl + ZnCl₂.

cards.term: Figure 2.8 · Dry cell
Dry cell electrode reactions and voltage?
cards.definition: Anode: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Cathode: MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃. About 1.5 V.

cards.term: Change in Mn oxidation state in a dry cell? Fate of NH₃?
cards.definition: +4 → +3; NH₃ complexes Zn²⁺ as [Zn(NH₃)₄]²⁺

cards.term: Mercury cell: electrodes, electrolyte, use?
cards.definition: Anode Zn–Hg amalgam cathode HgO + carbon paste electrolyte KOH + ZnO paste hearing aids, watches

cards.term: Mercury cell overall reaction and voltage?
cards.definition: Zn(Hg) + HgO → ZnO + Hg; 1.35 V

cards.term: Why is the mercury cell voltage constant over its life?
cards.definition: No ion in solution appears in the overall reaction, so no concentration term changes

cards.term: Lead storage battery: anode, cathode, electrolyte?
cards.definition: Anode Pb; cathode grid of Pb packed with PbO₂; 38% H₂SO₄

cards.term: Figure 2.10 · Lead storage battery

masks.answer: Negative plates: lead grids filled with spongy lead
Positive plates: lead grids filled with PbO₂

cards.text: Lead storage discharge: anode {{c1::Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻}}; cathode {{c2::PbO₂ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O}}.

cards.term: Overall lead storage reaction (discharge)?
cards.definition: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O

cards.term: What happens on recharging a lead storage battery? (Intext 2.13)
cards.definition: Reaction reverses: PbSO₄ → Pb at anode, PbO₂ at cathode; H₂SO₄ regenerated

cards.term: Why does acid density drop as a car battery discharges? (intuition)
cards.definition: H₂SO₄ is used up and water formed; mechanics check charge with a hydrometer

cards.term: Ni–Cd cell: vs lead storage, and overall reaction (NCERT)?
cards.definition: Longer life, costlier; Cd + 2Ni(OH)₃ → CdO + 2Ni(OH)₂ + H₂O

cards.term: Update: how is the Ni–Cd discharge usually written now?
cards.definition: Cd + 2NiO(OH) + 2H₂O → Cd(OH)₂ + 2Ni(OH)₂ (alkaline, KOH)

cards.term: What is a fuel cell?
cards.definition:
Galvanic cell converting combustion energy of fuels (H₂, CH₄, CH₃OH) directly to electricity.
Reactants are fed continuously

cards.term: H₂–O₂ fuel cell: electrodes, electrolyte, catalyst?
cards.definition: Porous carbon electrodes concentrated NaOH finely divided Pt or Pd

cards.term: Where was the H₂–O₂ fuel cell used? Bonus?
cards.definition: Apollo space programme; the water was drunk by astronauts

cards.term: Efficiency: fuel cell vs thermal plant?
cards.definition: Fuel cell ~70%; thermal plant ~40%

cards.term: Intuition: why is a fuel cell more efficient than burning fuel?
cards.definition: It skips heat → steam → turbine; each conversion step wastes energy (heat engines are Carnot-limited)

cards.term: Fuels other than H₂ in fuel cells? (Intext 2.14)
cards.definition: Methane, methanol

cards.term: Hydrogen economy (box)?
cards.definition: H₂ from solar splitting of water, burnt in fuel cells: product only water; both steps are electrochemical

cards.term: Examples of corrosion?
cards.definition: Rusting of iron, tarnishing of silver, green coating on copper and bronze

cards.term: Rusting as an electrochemical cell: anode and cathode reactions?
cards.definition: Anode spot: 2Fe → 2Fe²⁺ + 4e⁻ (−0.44 V). Cathode spot: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (1.23 V).

cards.term: E°cell for rusting?
cards.definition: 1.23 − (−0.44) = 1.67 V

cards.term: Source of H⁺ for rusting?
cards.definition: H₂CO₃ from dissolved CO₂ (and other acidic oxides)

cards.term: Composition of rust?
cards.definition: Hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (Fe²⁺ oxidised further by air)

cards.term: Intuition: why does rust form away from where the metal is eaten?
cards.definition:
One drop is a mini galvanic cell.
Electrons travel through the iron from the anodic pit to a cathodic spot where O₂ is abundant

cards.term: Why does salt water (sea air) speed up rusting?
cards.definition: Dissolved ions make the water a better electrolyte, completing the mini cell

cards.term: Ways to prevent corrosion?
cards.definition: Barrier: paint, chemicals (bisphenol), coating with Sn/Zn. Electrochemical: sacrificial electrode of Mg or Zn.

cards.term: How does a sacrificial anode work?
cards.definition: A more reactive metal (Mg, Zn, lower E°) is oxidised instead of iron, pushing electrons into the iron

cards.term: Galvanised (Zn) vs tin-plated iron when scratched? (teacher trap)
cards.definition: Zinc still protects (Zn is more reactive). Tin makes it worse: Fe becomes the anode next to Sn.

cards.term: Electrochemistry formula sheet
cards.definition: Cell emf: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; Nernst (298 K): E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q; Gibbs energy: ΔG° = −nFE°; Equilibrium: log K = nE°/0.059; Conductivity: κ = G*/R; Molar conductivity: Λm = 1000κ/M; Faraday: m = (M/nF)·It
